title: Nestlé CEO Philipp Navratil says employees need more than prompt engineering skills in AI era: What should they learn?
source_used: Business Insider (Ana Altchek, 8 Oct 2026), the original interview that Livemint rewrote; context from The Next Web, 8 Oct 2026
key_facts: Nestlé chief executive Philipp Navratil, who oversees more than 270,000 employees worldwide, told Business Insider that getting good at prompting AI is not enough for workers.
Workers still need to understand their business and how to use AI tools, and also need a bigger-picture understanding of AI itself, though not every technical aspect.
He said people need to understand what AI is capable of, what the trends are and how it can change anything at the company.
Too many people treat AI as just another tool instead of something that should fundamentally change how they work; the opportunity is rethinking workflows and processes around AI.
If employees use the tools they are given without changing their approach, AI may add layers of complexity instead of making work simpler.
Workers should rethink how AI can streamline processes and eliminate unnecessary work, freeing time to analyse data, meet business partners and move the business faster.

The Next Web adds that Navratil became CEO on 1 Sep 2025, that Nestlé announced plans weeks later to cut about 16,000 jobs over two years with automation of processes part of the plan, and that about 100,000 employees use Microsoft Copilot each month (per its CIO, to Fortune in January).
Livemint rewrote the Business Insider interview on 11 Oct 2026; the underlying interview was published on 8 Oct 2026.
quote_evidence: In today's workforce, getting good at prompting AI isn't enough.

"You need to understand what is it is capable of, what the trends are, what is happening, how AI can change anything at the company," the CEO of Nestlé, which owns brands like Nespresso and DiGiorno, told Business Insider.
He said if employees simply use the tools they're given without changing their approach, AI may add more layers of complexity instead of making work simpler.
why_it_matters_hint: The head of a company with more than 270,000 staff tells workers what he expects of them with AI: understand it and redesign their work, not just prompt it.
event_date: Business Insider published the interview on 8 Oct 2026 09:38 UTC; Livemint's rewrite is dated 11 Oct 2026.
